sources.citation: Wangka Maya Pilbara Aboriginal Language Centre. 'Kurrama' language page and 'Speaking, Reading and Writing Pilbara Languages' brochure (web, accessed 2026-09-17).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Language page: Dench worked with the Kurrama Elders Group from 1990; his texts were used in 2006 to produce the Kurrama Dictionary and Sketch Grammar; fewer than 10 speakers in 2002. Brochure: generic sounds/syllables primer for Pilbara languages; nothing on stress (scanned of page 2 checked).

sources.citation: Thieberger, Nicholas. 1993. Handbook of Western Australian Aboriginal languages south of the Kimberley Region. Pacific Linguistics C-124. Entry 4.4.5 Kurrama, pp. 115-116; annotated bibliography pp. 310-311, 329.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Bibliographic handbook, no phonology. States 'Grammar or sketch grammar: None, but see Wordick's (1982) grammar of Yindjibarndi, which is very closely related to Kurrama'; 'Practical spelling system: None, but the Yindjibarndi system may be used'; cites Dench (1990 p.c.) that Kurrama and Yindjibarndi are 'phonologically, morphologically and syntactically very similar' and names five dialects (Yarnarri, Yinyjiwarnti Kurrama, Mijarranypa, Marntartka, Ngamangamara). Lists Hale 1959 'Gurama fieldnotes' MS, Dench 1990 MS wordlist/texts, Dench 1987a Appendix A comparative phonology. Nothing on stre…

sources.citation: Dench, Alan. 1987. Martuthunira: a language of the Pilbara region of Western Australia. PhD thesis, Australian National University. Appendix A 'The phonological history of the Ngayarda languages', A.3 'Phonological changes in Kurrama', pp. 522-523; sec. 2.6 Stress pp. 97-105 (Martuthunira).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: The only Kurrama-specific phonology is diachronic (stop lenition parallels Yindjibarndi; syllable-final laterals fortify to stops: *pulka > putka, *wirlkara > wirtkaa, *-lkaji > -tkayi). The stress section (2.6) is about Martuthunira (initial stress, disyllabic pattern, lexical stress marks). No statement about Kurrama stress.

sources.citation: Wordick, F. J. F. 1982. The Yindjibarndi language. Pacific Linguistics C-71. Canberra: ANU. sec. 1.1.4 (p. 6) and sec. 2.3.2 'Accent' (pp. 41-42).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Describes YINDJIBARNDI accent only: within the word, stress and pitch combine into three degrees; in words with short vowels the pattern is 1 3 2 3 2 3 (primary on syllable 1, secondary on odd syllables), long vowels in even syllables attract the accent. On Kurrama it says (p. 6) 'The two languages possess identical phonological systems' but 'I have not included a description of Kurrama in this book.' No Kurrama stress statement — the earlier scan's hope that this grammar covers Kurrama is not borne out.
